notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Esther 3, based on the sources I was able to access.

---

## Esther 3 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — Haman's Promotion

**Traditional Reading (Multiple Sources)**

- **Timing**: Gill notes this occurred "five years after" Esther's marriage (citing Aben Ezra), or at least more than four years after, based on Esther 3:7. The Pulpit Commentary estimates about 476–475 BC.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/3.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-3.html
- **"Haman … the Agagite"**: David Guzik and Grant both identify Haman as a descendant of Agag, king of the Amalekites (1 Samuel 15:8), making him a hereditary enemy of Israel (Exodus 17:14-16). Guzik adds that "no self-respecting Benjaminite would bow before a descendant of the ancient Amalekite enemy of the Jews" (quoting Huey).
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-3/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/esther-3.html
- **Ellicott's caution**: Ellicott notes that Haman's name and his father's are Persian, making "Agagite" difficult. He points out that after the wholesale destruction of Amalek in 1 Samuel 15, it is "hard to see how … any members should have been left of the kingly family, maintaining a distinct tribal name for so many centuries." He notes that the Greek Apocryphal additions to Esther call Haman a Macedonian. The Pulpit Commentary likewise says "most probably the term used was a local one, marking the place of Haman's birth."
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/3.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-3.html
- **Gill's alternate view**: Gill records that some rabbis (Aben Ezra) identify Haman with Memucan from Esther 1:14. He also notes the Targums and Josephus make Haman a descendant of Amalek.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/3.htm
- **Elevation**: The Pulpit Commentary says Haman became "grand vizier" or chief minister, with his throne set above all other princes. Gill adds that Persian kings customarily advanced those they thought "best deserved it" to the highest seats.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-3.html

**Denominational Distinctive – Baptist**

- The **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** remarks that "a period of five years had expired between the crowning of Esther and Haman's exaltation, in which the nationality of Esther was kept secret."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/esther-3.html

---

### vv. 2–3 — Mordecai's Refusal to Bow

**Traditional Reading**

- **Nature of the homage**: Gill argues that the required homage was more than mere civil honour, because (a) the king had to issue a special command for it — which would be superfluous for ordinary respect — and (b) Jews did not refuse ordinary prostration (e.g. 1 Samuel 24:8; 1 Kings 1:16). Gill concludes that divine honours were being demanded. Ellicott agrees: Mordecai's objection was "mainly on religious grounds, as giving to a man Divine honours (Josephus)," and the fact that Mordecai cited his Jewish identity (v.4) confirms this.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/3.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/3.htm
- **The Pulpit Commentary** notes that Greeks occasionally refused to prostrate before the Great King himself, saying "it was not their custom to worship men" (citing Herodotus 7.136; Plutarch; Arrian), and Mordecai had the same scruple. Prostration was an act of worship, and only God should receive it.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-3.html
- **David Guzik** takes a slightly different line: "There does not seem to be a Biblical command against bowing or paying homage to a political leader as a sign of respect." Rather, Mordecai "must have known something about this man Haman, which persuaded him that Haman was unworthy of such honour." He locates the refusal in personal integrity rather than a specific scriptural prohibition.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-3/
- **"Why do you transgress the king's command?"**: Guzik notes that no specific command from the king is recorded; the command may have been implied by Haman's promotion.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-3/

**Denominational Distinctive – Baptist**

- The **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** speculates that "perhaps even the Persians were galled at the necessity to bow before the haughty Haman, and resented Mordecai's escaping the requirement."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/esther-3.html

---

### v. 4 — The Servants' Persistence and Report to Haman

**Traditional Reading**

- **"Day after day they warned him"**: Gill says they pressed Mordecai daily, "putting him in mind of his duty to obey the king's command, suggesting to him the danger he exposed himself to." The Pulpit Commentary suggests Mordecai eventually explained that "as a Jew, he was precluded from prostrating himself before a man."
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/3.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-3.html
- **"To see whether Mordecai's behavior would be tolerated"** (BSB) / **"whether Mordecai's matters would stand"** (KJV): Ellicott corrects the KJV — it should be "his words," meaning "whether his statement that he belonged to a nation who might only pay such reverence to God, would hold good." The servants were testing whether a religious exemption would be accepted.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/3.htm
- **"He had told them he was a Jew"**: This was Mordecai's sole explanation — his religious identity prevented the act. Gill calls it "a reason sufficient, because, by a fundamental law of his religion, he was not to worship mere man, but God only."
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/3.htm
- **Guzik**: Haman did not initially notice Mordecai's resistance — "it had to be pointed out to him by his aides."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-3/

---

### vv. 5–6 — Haman's Rage and Genocidal Response

**Traditional Reading**

- **"Filled with rage"**: Guzik describes Haman as "an extremely proud and insecure man; he could only consider himself a success if everyone else thought he was a success." The Pulpit Commentary adds that Mordecai's religious excuse likely made things worse: "if allowed, it would justify all the Jews in the empire in withholding from him the respect that he considered his due."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-3/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-3.html
- **Precept Austin**: Notes the pattern — "The emotion or thought (rage) leads to action or reaction (kill). Lesson: Be careful what you say and do when you sense you are under the control of your emotions."
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/esther_3-4_commentary
- **Genocide rather than individual punishment**: The Pulpit Commentary explains that Haman thought killing Mordecai alone was beneath him — too "low and mean a person only to wreak his vengeance on." He resolved to wipe out the entire nation. Gill adds that Haman also saw that "both by his example, and upon the same principle with him, they would all to a man refuse to give him reverence."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-3.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/3.htm
- **Historical precedent**: The Pulpit Commentary notes that large-scale massacres were not unknown in the Persian Empire, citing the massacre of the Magi on the accession of Darius Hystaspis (Herodotus 3.79) and a massacre of Scythians about a century earlier.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-3.html

---

### v. 7 — Casting the Pur (Lot)

**Traditional Reading**

- **"Pur"**: This is a Persian word for "lot" (the Hebrew word is added as explanation). The Pulpit Commentary connects it to Old Persian *pareh* and Latin *pars*. Haman used the lot superstitiously to determine the luckiest day for the massacre.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-3.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/3.htm
- **Providential delay**: The lot fell on the 12th month (Adar), giving nearly a full year before the planned massacre. Guzik, Gill, Ellicott, and the Pulpit Commentary all see God's providence here: "The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD" (Proverbs 16:33). Ellicott writes: "Thus in God's providence ample time was allowed for redressing matters."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-3/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/3.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/3.htm
- **Gill** notes that lots were cast "from day to day, and from month to month" throughout the year until the 13th day of the 12th month emerged — "the providence of God so overruling the lot, that there might be time enough for the Jews, through the mediation of Esther to the king, to prevent their destruction."
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/3.htm

**Baptist Distinctive**

- The **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** calls Haman "very superstitious and a practitioner of the cultic," adding that casting lots for guidance is "plainly condemned by Scripture (Deuteronomy 18:9-14; Colossians 2:16-19)." It also suggests — without endorsing — that "some think the modern superstition surrounding 13 stems from this."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/esther-3.html

---

### vv. 8–9 — Haman's Proposal to the King

**Traditional Reading**

- **Half-truths**: Guzik calls Haman's accusation "the most dangerous possible; it was a half-truth." Yes, Jews were scattered and had distinct laws, "but their own laws, to this point, did not prevent them from keeping the king's laws as loyal subjects."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-3/
- **Deliberate vagueness**: The Pulpit Commentary notes Haman never named the people — "he did not identify the people he intended to destroy, nor does the king appear to have considered it of enough consequence to inquire." Both Guzik and Grant agree: Haman neglected to tell the king how numerous these people were.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-3.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/esther-3.html
- **Dispersal**: Ellicott points out that most Jews had remained in the empire even after Cyrus's decree allowing return — only 42,360 had gone back (Ezra 2:64).
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/3.htm
- **Historical pattern**: Ellicott notes that the charge of disloyalty "has been a favourite weapon in the hands of persecutors," citing earlier accusations against the Jews in Ezra 4:13, 16, and the similar charge later levelled against early Christians.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/3.htm
- **10,000 talents of silver**: The Pulpit Commentary estimates this at "not much less than two millions and a quarter of pounds sterling" (late 19th-century value). Ellicott says it was "more than two-thirds of the whole annual revenue of the Empire" (citing Herodotus 3.95). Guzik and others note this was essentially a bribe and that Haman probably intended to recoup it from plundered Jewish property, though the edict later gave the spoil to the executioners (v.13).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-3.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/3.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-3/
- **Gill's alternative reading**: Gill notes that some scholars render "Haman said" (v.8) as "Haman *had* said" — suggesting Haman approached the king *before* casting lots, since he would need royal permission first. Gill himself leans toward the narrative order as given.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/3.htm

---

### vv. 10–11 — The King's Signet Ring and Consent

**Traditional Reading**

- **The signet ring**: The Pulpit Commentary explains this gave Haman "the power of making whatsoever edicts he pleased, since nothing was requisite to give authority to an edict but the impression of the royal seal" (citing Herodotus 3.128). It might have been a signet ring or a cylinder seal like that of Darius, now in the British Museum.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-3.html
- **"The enemy of the Jews"**: The Pulpit Commentary renders this as "persecutor" rather than "enemy."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-3.html
- **"Keep your money"** (BSB) / **"The silver is given to thee, the people also"** (KJV): The Pulpit Commentary clarifies: it is not that Haman's silver is returned, since it was never given — only offered. Rather, the king means "the silver of the people is given thee, together with the people themselves, to do with both as it pleases thee." Confiscation automatically accompanied execution in the East.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-3.html
- **The king's ignorance**: Guzik stresses that Ahasuerus "probably had no idea what he had agreed to; he probably believed that he had merely agreed to the execution of a handful of dangerous revolutionaries." Ellicott similarly describes the king's indifference as "incredible, but … quite in accordance with what we otherwise know of Xerxes" — too indolent to form his own opinion.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-3/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/3.htm
- **Gill** remarks that "it seems as if as yet Esther had not acquainted the king who her kindred and people were; or it can hardly be thought he would have so easily come into such a scheme."
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/3.htm

**Denominational Distinctive – Baptist**

- The **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** remarks: "This conduct of Ahasuerus certainly implicates him more fully in this attempt at genocide against the Jews. He can hardly be excused, though he later countermanded the law."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/esther-3.html

---

### vv. 12–14 — The Decree Written and Dispatched

**Traditional Reading**

- **The 13th of Nisan**: Ellicott notes that since the lot had fallen on the 13th of Adar, Haman may have chosen the 13th of Nisan as a corresponding date for issuing the decree. Bishop Wordsworth (cited by Ellicott) observes that this was "the eve of the Passover," creating a typological link: just as Haman plotted against the Jews on Passover eve, so centuries later "the Jews themselves, aided by heathen hands and the powers of darkness, sought to vanquish the Saviour" — and as the Jews of Persia were delivered, so Christ triumphed.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/3.htm
- **Scope of the decree**: Written to satraps, governors, and officials of every people — "in the script of each province and the language of every people." The Pulpit Commentary notes the Persian system allowed conquered peoples considerable self-governance under their own "head men."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-3.html
- **"Destroy, kill, and annihilate"**: The Pulpit Commentary observes that the edict, like a modern legal document, piles up "surplus words" for thoroughness.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-3.html
- **"Young and old, women and children"**: The Pulpit Commentary notes that killing the whole family of a criminal was standard ancient practice — even in Israel (Joshua 7:24-25) and certainly in Persia (Herodotus 3.119).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-3.html
- **"Plunder their possessions"**: This was an incentive for the populace to participate enthusiastically.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-3/
- **The courier system**: The Pulpit Commentary quotes Xenophon's description of the Persian postal system (Cyropaedia 8.6): stables with fresh horses and riders at day-intervals, operating day and night — "the most rapid of all methods of conveyance by land."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-3.html
- **Gill** notes that Haman had the decree issued so early (11 months before the date) partly to ensure it reached the farthest provinces and partly "lest Ahasuerus should change his mind, and be prevailed upon to revoke his grant."
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/3.htm

---

### v. 15 — The Couriers Depart; the King and Haman Drink; Susa is Perplexed

**Traditional Reading**

- **"Spurred on by the king's command"** / **"being hastened"** (KJV): Though there was ample time, the couriers were hurried — Haman feared the king might change his mind. The king may also have wanted the matter "settled past recall."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-3.html
- **"The king and Haman sat down to drink"**: The Pulpit Commentary likens this to Nero fiddling while Rome burned — "these two, having assigned a nation to destruction, proceeded to enjoy themselves." Guzik contrasts the two: "the king … thought he had done well – but he did not really understand what he had done. Haman also sat down to drink and thought he had done well – and he knew exactly what he intended to do."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-3.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-3/
- **"The city of Susa was in confusion"** (BSB) / **"perplexed"** (KJV): Ellicott explains the inhabitants "were puzzled and alarmed, as well they might be, at so marvellously reckless an order. Their sympathies, too, were clearly with the Jews and against Haman" (see Esther 8:15). Gill adds that many Persians were connected to Jews through affinity, friendship, or commerce and were "shocked at such a barbarous scheme." The Pulpit Commentary notes that as Zoroastrians, most Persians would naturally sympathise with the monotheistic Jews, and there may have been a widespread fear of the dangerous precedent being set.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/3.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/esther/3.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-3.html

---

## Points Where Protestant Traditions Differ

The sources I could access showed relatively little confessional divergence on this narrative chapter. The broad evangelical reading is shared across traditions. However:

- **Baptist** (Garner-Howes): Emphasises that casting lots for guidance is "plainly condemned by Scripture" and that the king bears real moral guilt. Sees a lesson that "the Devil is always scheming to frustrate the cause of Christ" and "the inhuman hatred of the Jews has not ceased to exist in this modern day."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/esther-3.html
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic** (Enduring Word / David Guzik): Locates Mordecai's refusal in personal integrity and discernment ("he knew Haman was unworthy") rather than strictly in Old Testament law prohibiting bowing. Emphasises the practical psychology of pride and insecurity.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-3/
- **Reformed** (Precept Austin): Strongly emphasises God's hidden providence — "God's Name is not mentioned once, yet God's 'Hand' is clearly present and active throughout the book, to the extent that many see the book of Esther as a veritable 'treatise' on the doctrine of Divine Providence." Connects Haman's rage to the New Testament teaching on being "filled with the Spirit" (Ephesians 5:18) as the antidote.
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/esther_3-4_commentary
- I was unable to retrieve distinct Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Methodist/Wesleyan (seedbed.com, wesley.nnu.edu), or Anglican commentary on this chapter.

---

## Other Views (Well-Known)

- **"Agagite" as Amalekite vs. Persian local name**: The traditional Jewish and early Christian view (Josephus, the Targums, Gill, Guzik, Grant) treats Haman as descended from Agag of Amalek. The more critical view (Ellicott, Pulpit Commentary, Cambridge Bible) treats "Agagite" as most likely a Persian geographical term, noting the Persian etymology of Haman's name and the historical difficulty of Amalekite survivors. Readers may choose between these.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/esther/3.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-3.html
- I was unable to retrieve Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com), Orthodox (oca.org), or modern scholarly (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org) commentary due to search limits being reached.
